title: A Python client for a stock game

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine a stock-trading game where you want a script to check your portfolio every morning. The site has no official API. What do you do?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: More or less, but tidily. Antoine wanted to automate chores in MarketWatch's virtual stock game. It's paper trading, not a real broker. So he shipped a small Python package on PyPI called marketwatch.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Watchlists, listing games and reading their settings, positions and pending orders, buying and selling inside the game rules, and the leaderboard. You log in once with a class, then make many calls in a script.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why not just use curl scripts in a notebook?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two reasons. The game has session cookies, rules and leaderboards that change with the semester. And he wanted something documented for teammates. A shared gist rots the moment the HTML form changes. The package is intentionally small: no database layer, no strategy engine, just HTTP shaped like the site.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One explicit method per endpoint, so it's easy to search when MarketWatch changes a path. Docs on GitHub Pages, because the PyPI description is too short for login edge cases. And no bundled strategies, so the library stays neutral.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Install it with pip, create the client with a username and password, then call something like get games or get price for a ticker.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Honest ones. It's an unofficial API, so pin versions and expect breakage. Automation may conflict with the site's terms, so it's for learning, not abuse. And paper gains don't validate a strategy.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Small bots and screening inside the game. Not high-frequency trading, not brokerage. The full write-up links the docs and the source.
